Other signal processing methods are available in `StructuralVibration.jl`.

## Detrending

Detrending is the process of removing trends from a signal. This is useful when you want to analyze the fluctuations around a trend. The `detrend` function can be used to remove linear or polynomial trends from a signal.

### API

::: {.api}
**detrend**

data.text/html:
detrend(t, y, order = 1, bp = [])

Detrend a signal y with respect to time t using a polynomial of order order.

Inputs

  • t: Time vector

  • y: Signal to be detrended

  • order: Order of the polynomial (default is 1)

  • bp: Breakpoints for the polynomial (default is empty)

Output

  • y_detrended: Detrended signal

Notes

order can be a vector if the trend is different over the segments defined by the breakpoints bp.

The breakpoints bp are the points where the polynomial order changes. If bp is empty, a single polynomial is fitted to the entire signal.
data.text/markdown:
```julia
detrend(t, y, order = 1, bp = [])
```

Detrend a signal `y` with respect to time `t` using a polynomial of order `order`.

**Inputs**

  * `t`: Time vector
  * `y`: Signal to be detrended
  * `order`: Order of the polynomial (default is 1)
  * `bp`: Breakpoints for the polynomial (default is empty)

**Output**

  * `y_detrended`: Detrended signal

**Notes**

`order` can be a vector if the trend is different over the segments defined by the breakpoints `bp`.

The breakpoints `bp` are the points where the polynomial order changes. If `bp` is empty, a single polynomial is fitted to the entire signal.

source:
#| output: false
# Signal 1
x1 = -0.5:0.01:0.5
y1 = @. sin(π*x1) + 0.25
y1_const = detrend(x1, y1, 0)
y1_lin = detrend(x1, y1, 1)

# Signal 2
x2 = 0:0.1:20
y2 = @. 3sin(x2) + x2
y2_const = detrend(x2, y2, 0)
y2_lin = detrend(x2, y2, 1)

#| echo: false
fig = Figure()
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], ylabel = "signal", title = "sin(πt) + 0.25")
ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1], xlabel = "x", ylabel = "signal", title = "3sin(x) + x")
hlines!(ax1, 0, color = :black, linewidth = 0.5)
vlines!(ax1, 0, color = :black, linewidth = 0.5)
lines!(ax1, x1, y1, label = "Original")
lines!(ax1, x1, y1_const, label = "Constant trend")
lines!(ax1, x1, y1_lin, label = "Linear trend")
xlims!(ax1, x1[1], x1[end])

hlines!(ax2, 0, color = :black, linewidth = 0.5)
lines!(ax2, x2, y2, label = "Original")
lines!(ax2, x2, y2_const, label = "Constant trend")
lines!(ax2, x2, y2_lin, label = "Linear trend")
xlims!(ax2, x2[1], x2[end])

Legend(fig[:, 2], ax1)

display(fig);

## Gradient

The gradient of a signal is the rate of change of the signal with respect to time. Julia [![](/assets/logo/julia.svg){width=4mm}] has a lot of packages for computing the gradient of a signal. The `gradient` function in `StructuralVibration.jl` is a simple helper function built around the `gradient` function in `Interpolations.jl`.

### API

::: {.api}
**gradient**

data.text/html:
gradient(f::Vector{Real}, t; method = :cubic)
gradient(f::Matrix{Real}, t; method = :cubic, dims = 1)

Compute the gradient of a function f at points t.

Inputs

  • f: Function values

  • t: Points at which to evaluate the gradient

  • method: Interpolation method

    • :linear: Linear interpolation

    • :cubic: Cubic spline interpolation (default)

  • dims: Dimension along which to compute the gradient

    • 1: Rows (default)

    • 2: Columns

Output

  • df: Gradient of the vector f at points t

Note

If method is :cubic, t must be an AbstractRange.
data.text/markdown:
```julia
gradient(f::Vector{Real}, t; method = :cubic)
gradient(f::Matrix{Real}, t; method = :cubic, dims = 1)
```

Compute the gradient of a function `f` at points `t`.

**Inputs**

  * `f`: Function values
  * `t`: Points at which to evaluate the gradient
  * `method`: Interpolation method

      * `:linear`: Linear interpolation
      * `:cubic`: Cubic spline interpolation (default)
  * `dims`: Dimension along which to compute the gradient

      * `1`: Rows (default)
      * `2`: Columns

**Output**

  * `df`: Gradient of the vector `f` at points `t`

**Note**

If `method` is `:cubic`, `t` must be an `AbstractRange`.

#| output: false
# Signal
x = LinRange(0., 3π, 100)
y = sin.(x)

# True gradient
dy = cos.(x)

# Estimated gradient
dy_approx = gradient(y, x)

#| echo: false
fig1 = Figure()
ax1 = Axis(fig1[1, 1], xlabel = "x", ylabel = "signal")
lines!(ax1, x, dy, label = "cos(x)")
lines!(ax1, x, dy_approx, linestyle = :dash, label = "gradient")
xlims!(ax1, x[1], x[end])
axislegend(ax1, position = :rt)

display(fig1);

::: {.callout-note}
Being based on interpolation, `gradient` is not robust against noise. For robust gradient estimation, you can compute the gradient of the signal denoised by the `denoising` function by using one of the numerous Julia differentiation packages if the signal is smooth enough (at least class $C^\2$). If the latter condition is not satisfied, you can for instance use [NoiseRobustDifferentiation.jl](https://adrianhill.de/NoiseRobustDifferentiation.jl/stable/), which implements the Total variation regularized numerical differentiation method[^1] .

[^1]: R. Chartrand. "Numerical differentiation of noisy, nonsmooth data". ISRN Applied Mathematics, vol. 2011, 164564, 2011.
:::
## Decibel conversion

The `to_dB` function converts a signal to decibels with respect to a reference value. Two cases must be distinguished:

* **Amplitude (root-power) quantities** (displacement, velocity, acceleration, pressure, FRF, RMS values, ...):
$$
L = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{|X|}{X_{ref}}\right)
$$

* **Power (energy) quantities** (squared amplitude, power, energy, PSD, autospectrum, ...):
$$
L = 10 \log_{10}\left(\frac{|X|}{X_{ref}}\right)
$$

In both cases, $X_{ref}$ is expressed in the same unit as $X$. For a power quantity, the reference is therefore the square of the amplitude reference, so that both definitions lead to the same level.

Usual reference values can be obtained with the `ref_dB` function.

### API

::: {.api}
**to_dB**

data.text/html:
to_dB(x, ref = 1.; type = :amplitude)

Convert a signal x to decibels (dB) with respect to the reference value ref.

Inputs

  • x: Signal to convert (scalar or array, real or complex)

  • ref: Reference value, expressed in the same unit as x (default: 1.)

  • type: Type of quantity contained in x

    • :amplitude (default): Root-power (field) quantity - displacement, velocity, acceleration, pressure, FRF, RMS values, ...

      L = 20 log₁₀(|x|/ref)

    • :power: Power (or energy) quantity - squared amplitude, power, energy, PSD, autospectrum, ...

      L = 10 log₁₀(|x|/ref)

Output

  • L: Level of x in dB

Notes

Both definitions give the same level for a given physical quantity, provided that ref is consistent with x. For a power quantity, ref must therefore be a power reference, i.e. the square of the amplitude reference (e.g. ref = (2e-5)^2 Pa² for a pressure autospectrum).

Usual reference values are given by ref_dB.

Null values of x give -Inf dB.
data.text/markdown:
```julia
to_dB(x, ref = 1.; type = :amplitude)
```

Convert a signal `x` to decibels (dB) with respect to the reference value `ref`.

**Inputs**

  * `x`: Signal to convert (scalar or array, real or complex)
  * `ref`: Reference value, expressed in the same unit as `x` (default: 1.)
  * `type`: Type of quantity contained in `x`

      * `:amplitude` (default): Root-power (field) quantity - displacement, velocity, acceleration, pressure, FRF, RMS values, ...

        L = 20 log₁₀(|x|/ref)
      * `:power`: Power (or energy) quantity - squared amplitude, power, energy, PSD, autospectrum, ...

Usual reference values are given by `ref_dB`.

Null values of `x` give `-Inf` dB.

       L = 10 log₁₀(|x|/ref)

  [1mOutput[22m

    [34m• [39m [36mL[39m: Level of [36mx[39m in dB

  [1mNotes[22m

  Both definitions give the same level for a given physical quantity, provided
  that [36mref[39m is consistent with [36mx[39m. For a power quantity, [36mref[39m must therefore be a
  power reference, i.e. the square of the amplitude reference (e.g. [36mref =[39m
  [36m(2e-5)^2[39m Pa² for a pressure autospectrum).

  Usual reference values are given by [36mref_dB[39m.

  Null values of [36mx[39m give [36m-Inf[39m dB.

L_amp = to_dB(1e-3, 1e-6)

# Same quantity expressed as a power quantity (ref = (1 µm/s²)²)
L_pow = to_dB((1e-3)^2, (1e-6)^2, type = :power)

# Using the usual reference values
L_ref = to_dB(1e-3, ref_dB(:acceleration))
